look_here_first: GIANT CUTGRASS: look for a TALL coarse rhizomatous emergent marsh grass, broad saw-edged blades and an unusually large open to drooping many-branched panicle. Its separate MALE and FEMALE one-flowered spikelets occur on the SAME panicle branches; in this species the MALE spikelets are BELOW the female spikelets on a branch (the opposite of eastern gamagrass's mixed-sex spike). Find the true LONG papery MEMBRANOUS ligule at a fresh blade–sheath junction, Kew usually 6–20 mm — not a tiny hair fringe. Confirm actual sex characters/spikelets with hand lens and mm scale. One Florida source photograph documents flowering-head form, not a Hays locality voucher.

best_field_traits: Very robust rhizomatous perennial rooted in fresh or mildly brackish marshes, ponds and stream banks; source-based, no new county occurrence claim.
Reedlike 2–3 m flowering culms with long, broad, sharply serrulate-edged blades (Kew 50–150 cm × 8–22 mm).
Large generally open, often drooping panicle about 30–60 cm; multiple branches rather than a fluffy Phragmites plume.
Separate 1-flowered male and female spikelets occur on SAME panicle branches, staminate/male BELOW pistillate/female (Kew GrassBase). Their sexual identity requires reproductive macro.
Distinctive LONG eciliate membranous ligule at fresh blade/sheath junction ~6–20 mm; not short ciliate ligule characteristic of some other wetland grasses.
Female fertile spikelets usually 6–8 mm, short-awned fertile lemma (~2–3-mm awn), and absent/obscure basal glumes (Kew). Needs a true dissected macro.
Leaf-margin teeth are sharp; do not slide bare fingers along blade or pull protected aquatic vegetation.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: WHOLE rooted marsh stand with flowering culm and broad attached leaf from same plant; no unnecessary rhizome excavation.
10–20× backlit leaf-margin serrulations with true arrow direction and 1-mm ruler, no barehand rubbing.
TRUE long membranous ligule unfolded at blade–sheath junction with ruler (Kew 6–20 mm); clearly contrast hair-fringe of comparison grasses.

SAME panicle branch displaying lower MALE (staminate/anther-bearing) and upper FEMALE (pistillate/stigma or fruit) spikelets, each actually photographed and source-ID confirmed before individual arrows.
One mature 6–8 mm female spikelet with 2–3 mm lemma awn, true glume base, separate anthers and stigma photographed under ruler.
Side-by-side verified native lineage Phragmites, invasive Arundo donax, smaller Leersia oryzoides, and endangered Zizania texana without collecting rare river plants.
crew_field_check: FIRST: giant tall wetland grass in often pure stand, but this is only a habitat/growth-form clue.
SECOND: seek a very large, arching loose-branched head; do not mistake it for the dense feathery plume of Phragmites or the bulky Arundo plume.
THIRD: unfold fresh blade/sheath junction: Zizaniopsis has a remarkably LONG paperlike ligule, ~6–20 mm (Kew). Measure instead of imagining it from whole-plant photographs.
FOURTH: examine several spikelets on ONE branch under lens: separate MALE below and FEMALE above. Do not assume exserted anthers or other structures are visible in the one existing image.
FIFTH: compare real tiny rough-margin teeth in a leaf micrograph, then verify one-flowered, glume-reduced female spikelet and short terminal awn (not shown here).
SIXTH: prioritize no-disturbance identification around the protected San Marcos River Texas wild-rice; do not dig in, handle or collect Zizania texana.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Giant cutgrass Zizaniopsis has tall coarse marsh growth; BROAD sharp-serrulate blades; a great loose 30–60-cm panicle with distinct separate one-flowered MALE and FEMALE spikelets on each branch (male BELOW female); and an unusually LONG membranous 6–20-mm ligule. Phragmites australis can have a distinctly feathery soft panicle; includes Texas native and introduced lineages, so a single morphology photograph does not certify invasion status. Introduced Arundo donax has a robust fluffy plume, bamboo-like cane and different spikelet/ligule details. Leersia oryzoides is generally smaller and has much smaller flattened narrow rice-shaped spikelets and tiny backward-pointing leaf teeth. Protected Zizania texana is aquatic wild-rice endemic to the San Marcos River and must not be handled for photographs. Tripsacum's thick single flowering spikes carry male units ABOVE female bead-like joints, opposite the mixed sex positions along Zizaniopsis panicle branches. Use paired reproductive/ligule photos before final call.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Giant cutgrass — head → true papery ligule → male/female spikelets
steps: Look for tall robust marsh/reedlike grass, leaves with rough edges. Photograph whole culm and complete large arching open branching panicle, not an isolated head alone.
Inspect the existing photo 1: real green branched panicle and a neighboring broad blade. That leaf is NOT conclusively connected to the same panicle-bearing stem.
Carefully open a fresh leaf at the true sheath/blade junction, photograph its usually LONG 6–20-mm eciliate papery ligule against mm scale. Never arrow it from a distant foliage photo.

Photograph several mature spikelets on SAME panicle branch, recording male/staminate BELOW female/pistillate units (per GrassBase). Separate floret sex requires anthers/stigmas/fruit, not shape guesses.
Measure one mature female spikelet ~6–8 mm and the short ~2–3-mm fertile lemma awn. Photograph the true basal region to establish absent/obscure glumes.

Compare emergent Phragmites (potentially native or introduced), Arundo donax (introduced), much smaller rice cutgrass and protected Texas wild-rice. Do not disrupt the San Marcos River wild-rice habitat.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Long 6–20-mm paper membrane ligule + wide serrulate leaves + 30–60-cm open panicle and separate male-below-female 1-flowered spikelets are a stronger Zizaniopsis diagnosis than height or wet habitat.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: One existing Florida photograph does not prove Hays nativity or even that its broad blade attaches to the flowering culm. MALE BELOW FEMALE based on Kew GrassBase, not photoproven in this image. Protected Zizania texana must not be handled/dug for comparison. Use the exact CC image credits and no unsupported arrow labels.
